I see.
The data locations are quite "local" compared with the domain as a whole. What's the max.edge value and projection for the data&mesh? What's fm_crs(mesh) for each mesh?
The sf results seemed to look "better" in some way, but if the estimated range is similar to or even smaller than the max.edge value, then you should probably just increase the mesh resolution (decrease max.edge) to allow it to capture the spatial scale better.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Different lgcp() results in inlabru when using either 'sf' or 'sp' objects
parts:
Yes, the mesh is too coarse for what it thinks is needed by the data; it's essentially trying to make the mesh act like spatially iid variables and the local discretisation error has a strong influence. This should change if you decrease max.edge.  However, your data is very localised, so you might want to try a more adaptive mesh; start by setting "cutoff" to e.g. 5 km, supply the observation locations as "loc" argument to the mesh generator, and increase min.angle to 26. This may be enough with sufficient resolution around the observations, without increasing the computational cost too much. Also, print(mesh) will give some potentially useful information, e.g. how many vertices there are.

Finn

On Friday 26 January 2024 at 17:55:35 UTC+2 Finn Lindgren wrote:
Yes, the mesh is too coarse for what it thinks is needed by the data; it's essentially trying to make the mesh act like spatially iid variables and the local discretisation error has a strong influence. This should change if you decrease max.edge.  However, your data is very localised, so you might want to try a more adaptive mesh; start by setting "cutoff" to e.g. 5 km, supply the observation locations as "loc" argument to the mesh generator, and increase min.angle to 26. This may be enough with sufficient resolution around the observations, without increasing the computational cost too much. Also, print(mesh) will give some potentially useful information, e.g. how many vertices there are.

Finn
